name: JavaScript
year_note: Prototyped as Mocha in ten days in May 1995; first public as LiveScript in the Netscape Navigator 2.0 beta (September 1995); announced as JavaScript on 4 December 1995; JavaScript 1.0 shipped with Navigator 2.0 in March 1996.
tagline: The language of the web browser: Java-like syntax over Scheme-style functions and Self-style prototypes.
summary: JavaScript is a dynamically typed, multi-paradigm language created at Netscape to script web pages and standardized as ECMAScript. Behind syntax that was required to 'look like Java' it combines first-class functions and closures in the spirit of Scheme with prototype-based objects taken from Self, driven by a single-threaded event loop. As the only language every web browser runs natively it became one of the most widely used languages in the world, and with Node.js and Deno it also runs on servers.
history:
Netscape hired Brendan Eich in 1995 to add a scripting language to its Navigator browser; management required that it 'look like Java' while staying simple and object-based rather than class-based. Eich wrote the Mocha prototype in ten contiguous days in May 1995, taking its object model (delegation through a single prototype link) from Self and its first-class functions from Scheme. It first shipped publicly as LiveScript in the Navigator 2.0 beta in September 1995 and was renamed JavaScript in a joint Netscape–Sun announcement on 4 December 1995, a marketing link to Java that the two languages' designs did not share.

After Microsoft shipped its reverse-engineered JScript in Internet Explorer 3 (1996), Netscape took the language to Ecma International, whose ECMA-262 standard (June 1997) adopted the placeholder name ECMAScript. ES3 (1999) standardized regular expressions and try/catch, but the ambitious ES4 effort was abandoned in 2008 in favour of the incremental ES5 (2009). Faster engines such as Google's V8 (2008), Ajax-style web applications and Node.js (2009) turned JavaScript from a page-scripting tool into a general-purpose language.

ECMAScript 2015 (ES6) was the largest revision: classes, modules, let/const block scoping, arrow functions, promises, iterators and generators. TC39 has since published a new edition every June, adding async/await (ES2017), private class fields (ES2022) and more, and JavaScript has become the compilation target of languages such as TypeScript.
innovations: Brought first-class functions and lexical closures (from Scheme) to a mass audience
Made prototype-based objects (from Self) the object model of a mainstream language
Event-driven scripting of web documents through event handlers and the DOM
Object and array literal syntax that became the JSON data-interchange format
Made non-blocking, callback- and promise-based asynchronous I/O mainstream, in the browser and on the server (Node.js)

typing.notes: Implicit coercions are pervasive ("1" + 2 is "12", [] == false is true); === compares without coercion. Values carry types, variables do not.

influenced_by.note: 'Scheme-ish first-class functions'; Eich was recruited to Netscape to 'do Scheme' in the browser.
Management required it to 'look like Java'; also the name, `this`, the Date class and the primitive/object split (string vs String).
JavaScript 1.0's statement syntax was modelled directly on C.
Regular-expression syntax and semantics, and the push/pop/shift/unshift/splice array methods (JavaScript 1.2).
slice/concat methods (JavaScript 1.2); later iterators, generators and destructuring.
The function declaration syntax (Eich: "'function', eight letters, I was influenced by AWK") and the for-in statement.

influenced_by_external.name: HyperTalk (HyperCard)
influenced_by_external.note: Inspired the event-handler model of the original Netscape DOM (onclick and friends).

block-scope.note: let/const are block-scoped; the original var is function-scoped.

exceptions.note: try/catch/finally and throw; any value can be thrown.

coroutines.note: Generators and async functions are stackless (one-level) coroutines.

generators.note: function* and yield, modelled on Python's; async generators since ES2018.

pattern-matching.note: Destructuring of arrays and objects only; there is no match/case construct.

tail-calls.note: Required by the spec in strict mode, but only JavaScriptCore (Safari) implements them.

classes.note: Syntactic sugar over constructor functions and prototypes; #private fields since ES2022.

inheritance.note: Prototype chains; class ... extends since ES2015.

prototypes.note: Every object has a [[Prototype]] link; Object.create() sets it directly.

traits-mixins.note: Mixins via Object.assign() or class-expression factories; no dedicated construct.

abstract-data-types.note: Encapsulation through closures (the module pattern) and #private class fields (ES2022).

modules.note: import/export ES modules; Node.js long used CommonJS require().

actors.note: Web Workers / Node.js worker_threads: isolated event loops communicating by postMessage (host APIs, not ECMAScript).

async-await.note: Built on Promises (ES2015) and the event loop.

reflection.note: Property enumeration, typeof, eval, and the Reflect and Proxy APIs (ES2015).

hot-code-reload.note: Hot Module Replacement in bundlers and dev servers such as webpack and Vite (tooling, not the language).

milestones.event: Mocha prototyped in ten days (May); ships as LiveScript in the Navigator 2.0 beta (September); renamed JavaScript (4 December)
JavaScript 1.0 ships in Navigator 2.0 (March); Microsoft's JScript ships in Internet Explorer 3 (August)
ECMA-262 1st edition standardizes the language as ECMAScript; JavaScript 1.2 adds regular expressions
ES3: regular expressions, try/catch, switch and do-while standardized
ES4 abandoned; Google Chrome ships the V8 engine
ES5 (strict mode, JSON, property descriptors); first public release of Node.js
ES2015 (ES6): classes, modules, let/const, arrow functions, promises, generators
ES2022: class fields, #private members and top-level await

trivia: Eich later wrote that the Java influences, 'especially y2k Date bugs but also the primitive vs. object distinction', were unfortunate.
'ECMAScript' began as a placeholder: Ecma avoided the trademarked name JavaScript, Netscape would not transfer 'LiveScript', and in September 1997 TC39 kept the placeholder.
Netscape 2 opened a JavaScript console when you typed javascript: into the address bar; the prototype's original mocha: scheme still worked.

hello.notes: console.log is provided by the host environment (browser, Node.js, Deno), not by ECMAScript itself.

factorial.notes: Numbers are IEEE 754 doubles, exact up to 2^53; BigInt literals (10n) handle larger factorials.

shapes.notes: Objects delegate to a shared prototype made with Object.create(); ES2015 `class Rectangle extends Shape` is sugar for the same prototype chain.

signature.title: Closures and the event loop
signature.expected_output:
1: start
2: synchronous code always finishes first
3: promise callback (microtask)
4: timer callback (task queue)
5: resumed after await
signature.notes: Synchronous code always runs to completion, then queued microtasks (promise callbacks), then tasks (timers). await suspends only the async function, never the thread, and `step` keeps its count in a closure.

browser.name: Native browser JavaScript engine
browser.notes: Runs natively in every browser (e.g. in a sandboxed iframe or Web Worker, capturing console.log); no WebAssembly needed.

runtime.notes: All six snippets give identical output under Node.js 24 and Deno 2.9.
